ai-agent.definition: An AI system that takes actions on its own, such as calling APIs, writing code or sending emails.

agent-provider.definition: The company that hosts and runs the agent.

deployer.definition: The organisation using the agent for its own work.

prompt-injection.definition: Hidden instructions in content the agent reads, which hijack what it does.

api-keys.definition: Secrets that let the agent log into or call services.

tool-gateway.definition: A checkpoint that an agent's outgoing calls to tools and APIs pass through.

cdn.definition: Services in front of many websites that can see traffic patterns across them.

agent-id.definition: A label on an agent's activity that says who runs it and who to contact.

shutdown.definition: Any targeted action that stops an agent from continuing harm, from revoking a key to ending the process.

intro.title: Follow the Incident
body: An {gl:ai-agent|AI agent} has been hijacked and is causing harm across the internet. The first company to notice can block it, but can it stop it?
This demo walks through the same incident twice, so you can compare the two outcomes.
Run 1 shows today: with no shared way to report the agent, it keeps causing harm for days.
Run 2 shows the same incident with a {gl:shutdown|shutdown} process in place: a report reaches the party who can act within hours.
intro.footnote: About 5 minutes. All numbers are illustrative.

steps.note: A {gl:prompt-injection|hidden instruction} in the package takes over the agent's task.
The agent is using its normal access, so nothing looks unusual to {co:agentcore}.

steps.event: {co:github} spots odd key use and blocks {co:atlas}.
steps.note: {co:github} is now safe. But the agent is still running.

steps.event: {co:github} tries to warn someone and emails a generic support inbox.
steps.note: There is no standard way to reach the party that can stop the agent.

steps.event: {co:atlas} uses stolen keys at {co:stripe} to issue fraudulent refunds.
{co:cloudflare} sees the same agent pattern on 3 customer sites.
steps.note: {co:cloudflare} can see the pattern, but has no one to tell.

steps.event: {co:agentcore} finally triages the support ticket and stops {co:atlas}.
steps.note: Six days after the first service knew.

run2.title: Run 2: With a shutdown process
run2.screenTitle: A standard report reaches the party who can act
run2.stageBarLabel: The four stages of a shutdown
run2.assumption: This assumes agents carry a reliable ID saying who runs them. That doesn't widely exist yet. Other options include passing reports back along the chain, or a shared repository providers check.

evidence.text: Its own logs confirm unusual activity
{co:brightwave} confirms {co:atlas} was not meant to call {co:stripe}

run2.logTitle: Record of what each party saw and did

steps.event: {co:atlas} installs the same poisoned package from {co:npm}.
steps.note: A {gl:prompt-injection|hidden instruction} in the package takes over the agent's task.
The agent is using its normal access, so nothing looks unusual to {co:agentcore}.

steps.event: {co:github} blocks {co:atlas} and sends a standard {gl:shutdown|shutdown} report. An {gl:agent-id|agent ID} on {co:atlas}'s traffic says who to contact: {co:agentcore} ({gl:agent-provider|provider}) and {co:brightwave} ({gl:deployer|deployer}).
{co:cloudflare} adds supporting evidence: the same agent pattern seen on 3 sites.
{co:atlas} uses stolen keys at {co:stripe} before any action lands.
steps.note: Fast is not the same as instant.

steps.event: {co:agentcore} checks the report: the sender is identifiable, the evidence is specific, {co:cloudflare} corroborates it, and its own logs confirm unusual activity. {co:brightwave} confirms {co:atlas} was not meant to call {co:stripe}. Decision: act on this one agent instance only.
Time to act. How should {co:atlas} be stopped?

{co:cloudflare} confirms no new traffic from {co:atlas}. {co:stripe} and other key owners rotate the stolen keys. Every party logs what it saw and did. {co:github} gets confirmation back. {co:brightwave} can patch and ask for {co:atlas} to be restored.

effects.text: Confirmed there is no new traffic from {co:atlas}.
Rotated the stolen keys, as did other key owners.
Recorded the report, the checks it made and the action taken.
Recorded the decision. It can now patch the problem and ask for {co:atlas} to be restored.

choice.title: How should the agent be stopped?
choice.prompt: Each option has trade-offs. Pick one to see what happens, then try the others.
choice.afterPick: Try another option, or press Next to continue.

result.headline: {co:atlas} loses its login, but the harm continues
result.text: {co:atlas} loses access to {co:brightwave}'s systems, but it still holds the stolen {co:stripe} keys, which don't depend on its login. {co:stripe} refunds continue until the keys are rotated.
result.lesson: Narrow isn't enough if it's the wrong control point.

result.headline: The harm stops and nothing else is disturbed
result.text: Every outgoing call is blocked, including those using stolen keys. Harm stops. {co:brightwave}'s other agents keep working.
result.lesson: Narrow and at the right control point.

result.headline: The harm stops at once, but it leaves a mess
result.text: Harm stops instantly, but a {co:stripe} refund batch is left half-finished (money moved, records not updated), and {co:brightwave}'s normal software builds fail.
result.lesson: Decisive but messy: safe failure has to be designed in advance.

effects.text: Killed the {co:atlas} process. A {co:stripe} refund batch was left half-finished.

result.headline: The harm stops, but so does everything else
result.text: Harm stops, but all of {co:brightwave}'s agents go down, including unrelated ones.

effects.text: Suspended {co:brightwave}'s whole account. All of its agents went down.
